s: A solutions architect is designing the data storage and retrieval architecture for a new application that a company will be launching soon. The application is designed to ingest millions of small records per minute from devices all around the world. Each record is less than 4 KB in size and needs to be stored in a durable location where it can be retrieved with low latency. The data is ephemeral and the company is required to store the data for 120 days only, after which the data can be deleted. The solutions architect calculates that, during the course of a year, the storage requirements would be about 10-15 TB. Which storage strategy is the MOST cost-effective and meets the design requirements?
o: Design the application to store each incoming record as a single .csv file in an Amazon S3 bucket to allow for indexed retrieval. Configure a lifecycle policy to delete data older than 120 days.

Design the application to store each incoming record in an Amazon DynamoDB table properly configured for the scale. Configure the DynamoOB Time to Live (TTL) feature to delete records older than 120 days.
Design the application to store each incoming record in a single table in an Amazon RDS MySQL database. Run a nightly cron job that executes a query to delete any records older than 120 days.

Design the application to batch incoming records before writing them to an Amazon S3 bucket. Update the metadata for the object to contain the list of records in the batch and use the Amazon S3 metadata search feature to retrieve the data. Configure a lifecycle policy to delete the data after 120 days.
e: DynamoDB with TTL, cheaper for sustained throughput of small items + suited for fast retrievals. S3 cheaper for storage only, much higher costs with writes. RDS not designed for this use case.

w.y: "Millions of small records per minute", "low-latency retrieval", "store 120 days only" and "MOST cost-effective" decide it. DynamoDB handles high write rates with single-digit millisecond reads, and TTL deletes expired items at no extra cost.

o.A: One S3 object per tiny record means huge PUT request costs, and S3 has no indexed retrieval.
o.B: Correct: DynamoDB sized for the load with TTL removing items after 120 days.
o.C: A single RDS MySQL table struggles with millions of inserts per minute and the nightly delete adds load.
o.D: S3 has no metadata search feature to find a record inside a batch object.
